summary: Describes the Message Tracking Query Protocol, which is used with an SMTP tracking extension to find the path a message took and its current routing status within a messaging system.

plainLanguage.summary: MTQP lets a client ask a mail system where an SMTP message went and what happened to it. The client supplies a tracking identifier and secret, and the server returns tracking-status information.

questions: how to find the status of an email message
what is the message tracking query protocol
how does the mtqp track command work
how do i track an email message through smtp servers
subtitle: A text protocol for asking a mail system how an SMTP message was routed.

tldr.problem: A sender or recipient may need to learn the path a message took through a mail system and its current routing status.
tldr.mechanism: A client connects to an MTQP server and sends a TRACK command with the message's tracking identifier and a base64-encoded secret. The server returns MIME tracking-status data when the secret is valid.
tldr.outcome: MTQP works with an SMTP tracking extension and a tracking-status media type. RFC 3887 is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 8553 and RFC 8996.

today: RFC 3887 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2004. It has been updated by RFC 8553 and RFC 8996; it has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: MTQP's Role in Message Tracking
sections.content:
Message tracking reports the path a message took through a messaging system and its current routing status. MTQP is one part of a three-document solution: an SMTP extension provides tracking information, a message/tracking-status media type represents it, and MTQP lets a client query the information.

RFC 3887 defines the query protocol for messages sent over SMTP. It uses a line-oriented client-server exchange over TCP.
sections.plainLanguage: MTQP is the protocol a client uses to ask a mail system about a message. Other specifications define how mail servers collect and format the tracking information.

sections.title: Finding the Server and Exchanging Lines
sections.content:
An MTQP server listens on TCP port 1038. A client first looks up an SRV record using service mtqp and protocol tcp; if no SRV records exist, it looks up an address record.

Commands use case-insensitive keywords and end with CRLF. Lines may contain at most 998 characters before CRLF. Responses begin with a status indicator: +OK for success, +OK+ for success with more lines, -TEMP for temporary failure, -ERR for permanent failure, or -BAD for a protocol error. Multi-line responses end with a line containing a period; a leading period in data is doubled.
sections.plainLanguage: The client connects to port 1038 and sends short text commands. Each response begins with a code that distinguishes success, temporary failure, permanent failure and protocol errors.

sections.title: Server Greeting and STARTTLS Option
sections.content:
After the TCP connection opens, the server sends a greeting that includes /MTQP. A negative greeting includes a reason such as /admin or /unavailable. If the server has options enabled, it lists them in a multi-line response.

The RFC defines the STARTTLS option. A server must list it when STARTTLS is enabled and certificates are installed. It must include the required parameter if TLS is required for some domains it handles.
sections.plainLanguage: The server introduces itself and lists available options. If it offers STARTTLS, the client can request TLS before sending a tracking query.

sections.title: The TRACK Command and Its Response
sections.content:
The core command is TRACK unique-envid mtrk-secret. The tracking identifier comes from the companion SMTP extension, and the secret is base64 encoded. The server hashes the secret using SHA1 and compares it with the hash supplied when the message was sent.

On success, the server returns a multi-line MIME body of type multipart/related, with message/tracking-status subparts. Those parts report information such as an action and status. If the server has never seen the message, it may return an opaque action or a negative /noinfo response.
sections.plainLanguage: The client sends the message's tracking identifier and secret. If the secret matches, the server returns one or more records describing the message's status.

sections.title: Chaining, Timers and Pipelining
sections.content:
A firewall gateway can report only that a message was passed onward, or it can query mail hosts behind the firewall and return their information. Chaining is an administrative choice. A server that chains must respond within 2 minutes; if it cannot provide an answer by then, it should report that no further information is available.

A server's inactivity autologout timer must be at least 10 minutes. A client waiting for a response must allow at least 2 minutes, since the server may be chaining queries. Clients may pipeline commands, and the server processes them in order. STARTTLS must be the final command in a pipelined group.
sections.plainLanguage: A gateway may ask other mail hosts for tracking details before replying. The client must allow time for that work, and the server processes pipelined commands in order.

sections.title: The mtqp URI Scheme
sections.content:
The RFC registers the mtqp URI scheme for requests that query a tracking server. A URI identifies the server and includes a /track/ path, the message identifier and the secret. A non-standard port can be included after the server name.

The path keyword is case-insensitive, but the tracking identifier and secret are case-sensitive. The secret is base64 encoded; reserved slash, question-mark and percent characters in the identifier or secret are percent-encoded.
sections.plainLanguage: An mtqp URI contains the server, tracking identifier and secret needed for a query. An application can use the URI to construct the TRACK request.

sections.title: TLS and Tracking Secrets
sections.content:
All MTQP servers must implement TLS, although an administrator may disable it. When the client receives a positive STARTTLS response, it must begin TLS negotiation before sending another command. After the handshake, both sides reset the protocol state and discard knowledge obtained before TLS.

Without TLS, a snooper may replay a tracking request and learn message status. TLS protects one client-server hop, not tracking queries across every server in a chain. The RFC says security depends on the randomness and exposure of each message's secret.
sections.plainLanguage: The tracking secret can be overheard or replayed if the connection is not protected. TLS protects the connection to one server, while each server in a chain remains a separate hop.
